title: Enabling sustainable supply of the essential cancer medicines etoposide and teniposide in yeast.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: No data file could be opened. The article is closed access: science.org returns HTTP 403 for the article page and for both guessed supplementary paths (science.aef5438_sm.pdf, data_s1_to_s4.zip). Europe PMC flags isOpenAccess=N, inPMC=N, hasSuppl=N, hasData=N; the PMC identifier returned by the NCBI link step (PMC13634237) belongs to an unrelated nanomedicine review, confirmed by fetching its Europe PMC record. OpenAlex reports oa_status 'closed' and no repository full text (Chalmers record is metadata only; a site search for 'teniposide' returned nothing). Zenodo search on the DOI string returned 0 records. NCBI nucleotide search found only one plausibly related 2026 deposit from this plant, PZ369892 (Sinopodophyllum hexandrum NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase-2 mRNA, 2,076 bases, deposited 2026-08-02) - a single sequence, not a dataset.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything about the content: that the authors made more than 60 genetic edits using 45 heterologous enzymes, identified key glycosyltransferases, and reached 89% and 65% yields in the final chemical step. All of this is from the PubMed abstract and secondary news/search summaries. The existence and contents of supplementary 'data S1-S4' (mentioned only in the published erratum, PubMed 42879565 / doi 10.1126/science.aem9151) were never seen.

a1_downloadable.note: FAIL, and this is where it dies. The paper is subscription-only; science.org gives 403 for the article and supplement, there is no PubMed Central copy, no author manuscript, no Zenodo/Dryad deposit, and no accession series. The strain, titer and enzyme-screen tables exist only inside paywalled supplementary files.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Not verifiable, and likely FAIL on the paper's description alone. The natural label is product amount per engineered strain, measured by LC-MS (liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry); in metabolic-engineering papers this normally lives in figure bar charts and raw chromatogram files, so it would have to be reconstructed per strain and per compound rather than read from a column.

a3_inputs_present.note: Not verifiable. Enzyme coding sequences for the 45 heterologous genes are presumably listed in the paywalled supplement; only one related GenBank record (PZ369892) was found publicly, so inputs would mostly have to be chased by name.

a4_units_stated.note: Not verifiable - no file was opened. The abstract states percentage yields for the chemical step but nothing about units used in the strain data tables.

a5_enough_rows.note: Would also FAIL on scale even with access. The paper's own numbers - 45 heterologous enzymes, >60 genetic edits, a pathway built in a modest panel of engineered strains - put the labelled-row count in the tens to low hundreds, far under the ~1,500 rows (or ~400 for classification) the checklist requires. Exact count unverified.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: well under 1 GB if ever obtained
a6_fits_laptop.note: Whatever tables exist are small; size is not the problem here.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Cannot be checked at all - no download. The published erratum states that errors in raw data file data S4 and in main-text and supplementary figures were corrected, which means two versions of the numbers exist and I could not see either.

a8_label_provenance.note: Provenance would be fine in principle: titers come from direct LC-MS (liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry) measurement of yeast cultures, not from another model's output. This is the one killer that is not a worry.

honest_claim_h3: No claim is possible: no data from this paper could be obtained, so nothing could be modelled or checked.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use enzyme sequence and substrate structure to predict which sugar-attaching enzymes glycosylate podophyllotoxin-type plant compounds
plain_idea.train_on: The project considered would have trained on each tested sugar-attaching enzyme (a UDP-glycosyltransferase, which bolts a sugar onto a small molecule) paired with the compound it was tested against. Number of such pairs: unknown, never seen, but the paper's own figure of 45 heterologous enzymes caps it in the tens.
plain_idea.predict: Whether the enzyme attaches a sugar at the required position, and how much product the engineered yeast strain makes. The true answer would come from liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry of yeast culture extracts, reported inside paywalled supplementary files.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Metabolic engineers rebuilding plant drug pathways in yeast spend months screening enzyme candidates by hand, so a predictor of which sugar-attaching enzyme works on which scaffold would shorten that screen. None of that is testable here because the measurements are not public.

ml_idea: Considered and abandoned: predict glycosyltransferase activity and regioselectivity on aryltetralin lignan scaffolds from enzyme sequence plus substrate structure, using ESM-2 (a protein language model) embeddings for the enzyme and a molecular fingerprint for the substrate. Abandoned because the measurements are paywalled and, on the paper's own counts, number in the tens rather than the thousands.

effort.compute_note: Not estimated - no data was obtainable, so there is nothing to size. Compute was never the constraint for this paper.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Try to download the supplementary data files. One HTTP request: science.org returns 403, Europe PMC has no copy, Zenodo has none. That single check kills it in under a minute.

verdict_reason: Part A1 fails outright. This is a closed-access Science paper with no PubMed Central copy, no repository deposit, no accession series, and supplementary files that return HTTP 403; the strain titers and glycosyltransferase screen results that any model would need are unreachable. Even with access, A5 would fail - 45 enzymes and ~60 genetic edits yield tens of labelled rows, not the ~1,500 needed - and the labels would have to be lifted out of figures and raw chromatograms rather than read from a column (A2). Excellent biology, not an ML dataset.
